transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-20
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Amy Park (Saga CTO), Ravi Singh (Infra), Lila (PM), external consultant (unnamed)

Summary:
Quick intro, current infra & pain (cold starts, noisy neighbors), primary objective: evaluate Dedicated reserved nodes vs hosted for predictable latency during weekly batch spikes. Strong emphasis on tenant isolation, KMS integration, SOC2, and a 3mo pilot.

Topics: reserved GPU sizing, tenant fencing, warm pools/hotpools, cold start times, burst-to-hosted fallback, VPC/KMS, pricing model, timeline for pilot

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'll do a quick intro from redwood side, jonas is our solutions engineer who'll do the perf/ops questions. amy, do you want to kick off with what you're seeing?
[00:15] Amy: yeah sure, uh so we've got a pretty clear problem, our search and summarization endpoints have a big spike every monday after our nightly ETL, like 10x baseline for 20 minutes. right now we're on a self-hosted cluster... and cold starts and noisy neighbors are killing us, um latency jumps to 2.5s p95 which is too slow for product.
[00:34] Ravi: and to add, we need tenant isolation because some customers require that their data never be co-located with other tenants — legal/contract reqs. we're also under a 6 month roadmap to move critical workloads to a managed offering.
[00:48] Maya: got it. so primary goals — predictable p95 under load, dedicated isolation for certain customers, and a cost model that doesn't explode. does that sound right?
[00:57] Lila: yes, and also we want a transparent fallback plan if reserved capacity is saturated — we can't go down mid-spike.
[01:05] Jonas: quick question, what's your current model footprint? sequence lengths, typical token rates? rough numbers are fine.
[01:12] Amy: most calls are short — 64 to 256 tokens, occasionally 1024 for longer summaries. traffic is pretty bursty: 40 req/s baseline geo-distributed, monday spike to 400 req/s for about 15-25 minutes.
[01:29] Jonas: ok that's helpful. our dedicated product gives you reserved GPUs with tenant fencing. you can carve out pools (hot pools) for runners that stay prewarmed — reduces cold starts and KV cache warmup. you can also configure burst policies to fall back to hosted instances if your reserved pool hits max capacity.
[01:49] Ravi: how deterministic is that fallback? we have strict SLOs for certain customers and can't accept a random 30% increase in cost or increased latency during fallback.
[01:58] Maya: good point. the fallback is policy-driven — you can choose strict-no-fallback for isolated customers (they'll be limited to reserved pool), or best-effort fallback for nonsensitive traffic. when fallback happens requests go to pre-approved model variants in hosted infra, typically with a small latency delta but lower capacity guarantees.
[02:19] Amy: and locking down encryption? we need KMS/HSM integration — customer-managed keys — and audit logs for access and token-level traces.
[02:29] Jonas: yes we support customer-managed KMS in Redwood Private and Dedicated with your own key reference in the KMS. audit logs are available through the console and can be exported; there are pagination quirks in the UI sometimes but the raw logs are full fidelity.
[02:45] Speaker 1: (muffled) do you have SOC2?
[02:48] Maya: we do, we're SOC 2 Type II and have ISO in the roadmap. i'll attach the compliance pack after.
[02:55] Lila: pricing — how do you bill reserved capacity vs burst usage? we need to project monthly cost for 3 reserved pools and a burst buffer.
[03:04] Maya: reserved is essentially a flat commit for the node-hours you reserve. burst is usage-based at a higher per-token or per-node-minute rate. we'll share a spreadsheet that models different warm-pool sizes and estimated burst minutes.
[03:17] Amy: what about prewarming overhead — like how much GPU memory and slot overhead does a hot pool have? is it linear?
[03:25] Jonas: it's not perfectly linear — there's overhead for model KV caches, and warm pools can share some memory if model artifacts are compatible. for example smaller quantized variants reduce KV footprint so you can prewarm more instances. but if you want strict tenant fencing you pay the isolation delta.
[03:44] Ravi: put another way, we need numbers: p95 cold start from zero, p95 warm after KV warm, and cost per prewarmed slot. can you produce benchmarks with our model family?
[03:53] Jonas: absolutely, that's what i'd recommend as a next step. we can run a 2-hour runner simulating your Monday spike with the exact sequence length and batching distribution to give you p50/p95/p99 and E2E token costs.
[04:07] Maya: jonas will own the benchmark. i'll follow up with pricing and the security pack.
[04:13] Amy: another constraint, we have customers in eu and na and need data residency for eu customers. can you pin model serving to regions and still have a global fallback?
[04:23] Jonas: you can pin; fallback can be region-limited. if you pin and the region is saturated, fallback won't cross borders unless you explicitly allow cross-region failover. so you can keep eu data in eu-only serving.
[04:36] Lila: how about multi-tenant billing and metering? we need token-level cost attribution to each customer and per-route dashboards.
[04:44] Maya: console exposes token-level breakdowns and per-route dashboards; we also offer an exportable cost/usage API so you can do internal chargeback.
[04:52] Amy: wanted to ask about model variants — can we run a quantized variant in dedicated and keep higher-precision in hosted? we care about fidelity for top-tier customers.
[05:02] Jonas: yes, you can run different model variants on different pools. the runtime supports the same API surface so application code is unchanged. one caveat: output distribution changes slightly with aggressive quantization; we recommend eval sets and automated quality monitors when doing A/B rollout.
[05:19] Ravi: A/B is fine, but we need canary rules and auto rollback if eval drift exceeds threshold. is that in the platform?
[05:27] Maya: yes, rollouts and canaries are supported. you can tie quality regression alerts to prompt sets, and configure automatic fallback to previous version on regression.
[05:36] Speaker 1: (interrupting) any hard limits on concurrent KV size?
[05:40] Jonas: roughly depends on model size and quantization; we expose the KV footprint numbers in model profiles. we'll include them in the benchmark report.
[05:48] Amy: timeline — we want a pilot within 6 weeks. ideally a 3 month pilot with two reserved pools: one for critical customers (isolation, strict-no-fallback) and one for general traffic with fallback. can you support an overlapping staging and prod warm pool?
[06:03] Maya: yes, many customers do a staging hot pool + prod hot pool. provisioning lead time depends on region and node type; 3-4 weeks typical for dedicated capacity in popular regions, sometimes quicker if capacity available.
[06:19] Lila: follow-up on compliance: can we get a support agreement for retention of logs for 12 months? some customers require 12 months retention for audit.
[06:29] Jonas: log retention is configurable; we offer add-on retention for longer windows. the export mechanism allows you to push logs to your S3 with lifecycle rules.
[06:38] Amy: any gotchas for VPC peering and private endpoints? our infra team dislikes public egress.
[06:44] Ravi: yes we want private networking and control plane separation where possible.
[06:48] Maya: dedicated supports VPC peering and private endpoints; for Private (customer-managed) we can do an air-gapped or on-prem pattern but that increases setup time and footprint. for most, VPC peering with customer KMS keys meets security needs.
[06:59] Jonas: and one operational note — if you do strict tenant fencing you can't borrow capacity from other tenants in the pool; that means you need to size the reserved pool to cover the worst-case traffic for those tenants. you can still configure burst window for lower-tier tenants.
[07:16] Amy: ok, so we need sizing guidance — like how many A100-equivalent slots for 400 req/s at 64-256 tokens with 95p under 400ms. can you model that?
[07:26] Jonas: yes, with the benchmark we'll produce recommended slot counts and the expected p95. also show cost delta for tight isolation vs shared pools.
[07:35] Lila: pricing modeling question — do you charge for idle prewarmed minutes even if not used?
[07:40] Maya: reserved nodes are a flat commitment; yes you pay node-hours to keep them reserved and prewarmed. for bursted hosted usage you pay only on use. we'll show both in the spreadsheet.
[07:50] Amy: do you support GPU types beyond a100? we have some hw constraints in our private DC for on-prem path.
[07:57] Jonas: we support multiple accelerator types across Dedicated and Private. for on-prem you'll need to validate kernel compat; our SE team can help.
[08:06] Ravi: one more — telemetry and latency tracing. we need per-request traces including queue time, batching delay, inference time, and token generation time.
[08:16] Jonas: console tracing includes those breakdowns; we also expose raw traces to your tracing backend via OTLP. small caveat: batching adds a queue time that may inflate p50 while reducing cost.
[08:30] Amy: any security concerns during benchmarking? we will share sample payloads that contain pseudonymized customer text.
[08:38] Maya: that's fine; we'll sign an NDA and treat benchmark data per our data handling policies.
[08:44] Speaker 1: (unclear) what's the SLA for failover?
[08:47] Maya: Dedicated has SLA on availability; for cross-fallback to hosted, you are relying on hosted capacity so we recommend mixing protections and regional redundancy. we'll include concrete SLA numbers in the follow-up doc.
[09:00] Lila: can we automate scale-out of reserved pools if we hit sustained higher traffic for two hours?
[09:07] Jonas: autoscaling on reserved pools is limited — you can configure scheduled scaling and manual scale, and a limited autoscale for predictable patterns. autoscaling that brings up new reserved instances has provisioning lead time so it's not instant. for immediate spikes, fallback to hosted is the mechanism.
[09:24] Amy: ok let's talk PED (product expectation) — we want a PoC that proves we can keep p95 under 400ms for our critical customers during the Monday spike. if the benchmark shows this with a reasonable cost, we'll sign a 12 month reserved commitment.
[09:38] Maya: understood. jonas, can we scope that bench to match the 15-25 minute spike? and include both isolation and shared scenarios?
[09:45] Jonas: yes. i'll set up a runner with two scenarios: strict-isolated pool sized to target p95<400ms and shared pool with fallback. we'll also run a cost-per-token calc.
[09:56] Ravi: last technical note: do you support service accounts and RBAC for engineers? we need granular access controls.
[10:04] Maya: yes, RBAC and SSO (SAML/OIDC) are supported. you can tie roles to API keys and enforce tenant-level permissions.
[10:12] Amy: ok that covers most of it. can you also include a short risks list for the pilot?
[10:17] Maya: sure — we'll enumerate risks: capacity lead time, model fidelity drift with quantization, cross-region failover complexity, and cost volatility in bursts.
[10:28] Lila: perfect. thanks. any other questions?
[10:31] Speaker 1: no
[10:33] Maya: next steps recap: we'll share pricing spreadsheet + compliance pack, jonas will run benchmark and share results, ravi will send traffic CSV, schedule follow-up security deep dive.
[10:45] Amy: sounds good. thanks all.

End of transcript.
